newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTORCYCLING-THE BIKE THAT KING KENNY BUILT.
newsitem.headline: MOTORCYCLING-THE BIKE THAT KING KENNY BUILT.

text.p: The most talked-about motorcycle on the 500cc grand prix grid this season holds little allure for triple world champion Michael Doohan.
"I wouldn't want to climb on the thing," the Australian said after winning the Italian Grand Prix at the weekend.
"I want to race bikes, not develop them."
But if three times 500cc world champion and winning team owner "King" Kenny Roberts is right, his new Modenas KR V3 will be challenging the best before too long.

With an engine built by Tom Walkinshaw, boss of the Arrows motor racing team, the three-cylinder motorcycle brings together Britain's flourishing Formula One industry, one of motorcycling's biggest names and Malaysian money.
For Roberts, it is the face of the future. It is also a genuine challenge to the mighty Japanese.
"We wanted to design a total concept bike...the KR V3 has been created as a Formula One type of entity," he said before the bike's debut race at the start of the season.

"I believe this is the way racing has to go if it is to grow. It needs to be more like Formula One cars, with its own industry. This way the money comes back into the racing industry, rather than ending up outside."
Doohan, a Honda rider who never likes to sit on his laurels, agrees on that. "What Kenny has done is good," he said.
"By trying to beat the Japanese it should force them to develop their own bikes more."
There is no denying that Roberts has shaken up the sport, dominated by Honda for the past three seasons.

While the ambitious Arrows team caused a stir in Formula One circles by signing world champion Damon Hill, it was nothing to the shock sent through motorcycling when Roberts broke with Yamaha last year and began building his own bike.
Heralded as the most important new grand prix bike of the past two decades, the Modenas intends to challenge Honda, Yamaha and Suzuki who have won every 500cc title since 1973.
That is still some way off, however.
First, just like Hill's troubled Arrows, there are one or two fairly major problems to be ironed out.
"We're probably the slowest motorcycle on the race-track in terms of actual top speed," Roberts said in an interview. "But top speed is not the total picture."
Far from it. The bike also has problems with handling, riding quality and weight as well as over-heating.
The death of Malaysian business leader Yahaya Ahmed in a plane crash in February was also a huge blow.
Modenas stands for Motorsikal Dan Enjin Nasional Sdn Bhd, an ambitious Malaysian manufacturer whose motorcycle output is currently limited to 110cc scooters.
It is owned by Yahaya's Hicom Holding bhd which also controls the carmaker Proton.

"We're behind in development, we're behind in time scales and meetings and priorities and commitments," added Roberts, who described the project as "scary" but also "the most exciting thing I've done since I stopped racing".
"This season is really a development one. We're nowhere close to what we're going to be this time next year."
In fact, progress has been remarkable already.
Work started on the bike in secrecy in May 1996 with Roberts building his own chassis from scratch.
It made its race debut less than a year later at the Malaysian Grand Prix in April.
The first qualifying session for that race was the first time the bike had been put through its paces with no limits imposed on the rpm or the throttle.
Since then, the Modenas has caused a fair stir.
French rider Jean-Michel Bayle, who had his first ride on the bike in Britain in January, was eighth at Mugello after finishing in the points at the two previous races.
"We learned a lot this weekend and made a lot of progress," said Roberts. "You should see some big improvements from here."
"We should have a test bike up and running this week and that is going to make a big difference."
The team has moved its headquarters from Amsterdam to the English town of Banbury for closer ties with Walkinshaw, whose responsibilities cover engine development.
Roberts said he had little choice in leaving Yamaha after failing to convince the Japanese bosses that Honda, as has since happened, were about to raise their game.
"We'd seen a huge thrust from Honda coming and just were unable to get them to believe it," he said.
"When the (Japanese Yamaha) management changed it made it all more difficult and I just gave up."
The main difference between the V3 and the four-cylinder works Hondas and Yamahas is that the regulations allow Roberts's machine to be 15 kilos lighter than the others.

That advantage has not been banked yet, with the team struggling to lose the weight, but when the problem is resolved it should enable the lighter bike to be more manoeuvrable, easier to ride and offering a better delivery of engine power.
That is the theory but there is still a long way to go in improving the riding quality for Bayle and Roberts Junior.
"Kenny's suffering more than Jean-Michel," said Roberts. "His riding style on the bike is not working well yet. But we're having a real look, trying to get Junior comfortable."
